assessments.reasoning: The vendor identifies SQL as the language SQLite implements and describes variation in both directions: SQLite leaves out some standard features and supplies features of its own. That supports dialect as a descriptive classification. The release entry identifies the 3.46.0 SQL surface to which the classification applies. The guide gives a product-level description and does not date its own text to 3.46.0.

The release heading and changes document an SQL surface in SQLite 3.46.0, including a change to literal syntax and changes to SQL functions. This anchors the release-specific side of the classification. The language guide supplies the relationship to standard SQL. The two documents share vendor authority.

challenge.method: Check whether the parent relation equates SQLite with the catalogued 2023 ISO edition, or whether the guide purports to document conformance to that edition. Does the release entry compare its changes with an ISO edition or identify a particular standard feature omitted in 3.46.0?
challenge.results: Neither cited document makes that identification. The joint evidence supports a relationship to SQL at the language-family level. It supplies no edition-specific conformance finding, historical inventory of omissions, or assurance of interchangeability. It does neither. Its contribution is the release-specific SQL evidence. Treating any listed change as a departure from ISO SQL would exceed the comparison the vendor made.

limitations: This is a documented language classification at the vendor evidence revision. It does not imply full ISO conformance, certification, interchangeability, or applicability to other releases.
The missing edition designation finding applies to the cited characterization and release evidence.
The relation is a catalog classification. SQL conformance, certification, portability and unsupported releases are outside the claim.
